edits.definition: Isobars are atoms of different elements that have the same mass number but different atomic numbers. Because the atomic number decides both the identity of an element and its chemical behaviour, isobars are chemically very different substances that happen to share the same nucleon tally. For example, argon-40 (⁴⁰₁₈Ar) and calcium-40 (⁴⁰₂₀Ca) both contain 40 protons plus neutrons, yet argon has 18 protons while calcium has 20. Isobars therefore differ in their proton and electron counts, and in almost all their physical and chemical properties.
edits.walkthrough_append: Work one more pair to fix the pattern: ³¹₁₅P and ³¹₁₆S both carry mass number 31, yet phosphorus has 15 protons and sulphur has 16 — different elements, same A. Notice the bookkeeping: in isobars, different numbers of protons and neutrons are arranged so that the two sums match. A typical board question gives the atomic number and mass number of two atoms and asks whether they are isotopes, isobars or neither; answer by checking Z first, then A. Exam takeaway: same Z with different A means isotopes; same A with different Z means isobars — state both conditions explicitly, because naming one without the other loses the mark. Self-check: write the nuclear notation for calcium-40 and argon-40 from memory, then confirm that each atom still sums to 40 nucleons.

edits.definition: A separating funnel is a conical piece of laboratory apparatus with a stopcock at the lower end of its stem, used to separate two immiscible liquids that differ in density. The mixture is poured in and allowed to stand until the liquids settle into two distinct layers; the stopcock is then opened to run off the denser bottom layer. The method works on the principle that immiscible liquids do not mix, however vigorously shaken, and that the layer of greater density settles at the bottom. Separating an oil–water mixture and extracting a product from a reaction mixture are its standard laboratory uses.
edits.walkthrough_append: Practise the full procedure the way the exam expects it narrated: close both stoppers and shake the funnel, invert it once, open the stopcock briefly to release built-up pressure, then clamp it upright and let it stand until the boundary between the layers is sharp. Remove the upper stopper before opening the stopcock — otherwise a partial vacuum forms inside and the lower layer will not run out smoothly. Collect the lower layer in a conical flask and the upper layer in a separate beaker, labelling each. Exam takeaway: the technique separates immiscible liquids on density difference, and the denser layer always leaves first through the stopcock. Self-check: draw a labelled diagram — conical body, stopper, two layers, stopcock — and state in one line why kerosene and water separate by this method but kerosene and petrol do not.

edits.definition: Ionic bonding is the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, produced when a metal atom completely transfers one or more of its valence electrons to a non-metal atom. The metal atom becomes a positively charged cation, the non-metal atom becomes a negatively charged anion, and both attain the stable electron arrangement of a noble gas. For example, sodium (2,8,1) transfers its single outer electron to chlorine (2,8,7), forming Na⁺ and Cl⁻. The ions then arrange themselves into a rigid three-dimensional crystal lattice held together by strong electrostatic forces, as in sodium chloride.
edits.walkthrough_append: Now generalise the electron bookkeeping: magnesium (2,8,2) must lose two electrons, but each chlorine atom can accept only one, so one magnesium atom hands its two electrons to two chlorine atoms, giving MgCl₂ — the formula records the actual transfer. As a second step, trace why ionic compounds conduct electricity only when molten or dissolved: the ions are then free to move and carry charge, while in the solid lattice they are locked in fixed positions. Exam takeaway: an ionic bond is the electrostatic attraction between ions formed by complete electron transfer — the metal loses electrons to become a cation, the non-metal gains them to become an anion, and both reach a noble-gas configuration. Self-check: draw the electron dot structures for the formation of MgO and Na₂O, writing the electron arrangement of each atom before and after the transfer.

edits.definition: Atomic number (Z) is the number of protons present in the nucleus of an atom, and it is the true identity of an element — no two elements share the same atomic number. In a neutral atom the number of electrons equals the number of protons, so the atom carries no net charge. Mass number (A) is the sum of the protons and neutrons in the nucleus, and it is always a whole number close to the measured atomic mass. In the standard nuclear notation ᴬ𝑍X the mass number is written as a superscript and the atomic number as a subscript before the symbol.
edits.walkthrough_append: Apply the relation A = Z + n as a quick mental drill: an atom of sodium with 11 protons and 12 neutrons has Z = 11 and A = 23, written ²³₁₁Na. For an ion the proton count never changes — only electrons do — so the sodium ion Na⁺ still has Z = 11 but only 10 electrons, while its nucleus is unchanged. Exam takeaway: Z identifies the element and equals the electron count in a neutral atom; A = protons + neutrons; in notation, mass number sits above, atomic number below. Self-check: for ³⁵₁₇Cl and ³⁷₁₇Cl, state Z, A and the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in each, and explain why both atoms are still chlorine.

edits.definition: Isotopes are atoms of the same element that have the same atomic number but different mass numbers, because their nuclei contain different numbers of neutrons. Since chemical behaviour depends only on the number and arrangement of electrons, isotopes of an element show almost identical chemical properties while differing in physical properties that depend on mass, such as density and rate of diffusion. Hydrogen has three isotopes — protium, deuterium and tritium — and carbon occurs naturally as carbon-12 and carbon-14. Because the proton count is fixed for an element, no isotope can ever change one element into another.
edits.walkthrough_append: Place the three hydrogen isotopes side by side: protium has one proton and no neutron, deuterium has one proton and one neutron, tritium has one proton and two neutrons — all three have Z = 1, so all three are hydrogen. Ordinary hydrogen gas is almost entirely protium, which is why the measured atomic mass of hydrogen stays close to 1 u. Exam takeaway: isotopes share chemical properties because they share electrons, but differ in physical properties tied to mass; identify an isotope pair by equal Z and unequal A. Self-check: for carbon-12 and carbon-14, write the neutron count of each, predict which is denser, and justify why both take part in chemical reactions in exactly the same way.

edits.definition: Sublimation is the change of state in which a solid is converted directly into vapour on heating, without passing through the liquid state. The reverse change, in which the vapour is converted directly back into solid on cooling, is called deposition. Sublimation happens in solids whose surface particles gain enough energy to escape straight into the gas phase before the solid melts. Camphor, naphthalene, ammonium chloride, iodine and dry ice (solid carbon dioxide) are the standard examples, and the property is used to separate such substances from non-volatile impurities.
edits.walkthrough_append: Narrate the ammonium chloride–sand separation as a sequence: heat the mixture in a china dish, cover it with an inverted glass funnel whose stem is plugged with cotton, and the ammonium chloride vapours leave the dish, touch the cool funnel walls and deposit there as a fine white solid, while the sand stays put. The cotton plug stops the vapour from escaping through the funnel stem. Exam takeaway: sublimation skips the liquid state, so it separates a volatile solid from non-volatile ones — name camphor, naphthalene, iodine, ammonium chloride and dry ice as the expected examples. Self-check: explain why a naphthalene ball shrinks in a wardrobe without ever wetting the floor, and why ordinary salt cannot be separated from sand by this method.

edits.definition: Molecular mass is the sum of the atomic masses of all the atoms in one molecule of a covalent substance, expressed in unified atomic mass units (u). It is calculated by multiplying the atomic mass of each element by the number of its atoms shown in the molecular formula, and adding the results. For glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆, the molecular mass is (6 × 12) + (12 × 1) + (6 × 16) = 180 u. The calculation uses whole standard atomic masses, which is why the result is always an approximate whole-number value.
edits.walkthrough_append: Do one bracketed formula end to end so the exam version holds no surprises: for calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)₂, take calcium 40, oxygen 16 and hydrogen 1, so the molecular mass is 40 + 2 × (16 + 1) = 74 u — the subscript 2 multiplies everything inside the bracket. Then check yourself against glucose: 72 + 12 + 96 = 180 u, exactly the figure on the ORS packet. Exam takeaway: molecular mass is the sum of atomic mass times subscript over every element in the formula, in u; never forget the multiplier written outside a bracket. Self-check: compute the molecular masses of CO₂ and C₂H₅OH with one line of working each, and verify that your CO₂ answer comes to exactly 44 u.

Build the classification table methodically: clouds and fog are aerosols (liquid dispersed in gas), smoke is a solid aerosol (solid in gas), milk is an emulsion (liquid in liquid), butter and cheese are gels (liquid in solid), and ink or muddy river water behaves as a sol (solid in liquid). Test any dispersion with two questions — does it scatter a light beam, and does it pass through filter paper unchanged? Colloids pass through filter paper yet still scatter light, which separates them from both true solutions and suspensions in one stroke. Exam takeaway: colloid particles are 1–1000 nm across — individually invisible, too small to settle or be filtered out, yet large enough to scatter light. Self-check: classify fog, milk, jelly and ink by naming the dispersed phase and the dispersion medium of each.

Fix the numbers that exams ask for: the electron carries one unit of negative charge (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) and has a mass of about 1/1836 u — negligible beside the proton's roughly 1 u; the neutron matches the proton in mass but carries no charge, which is exactly why it left no trace in the cathode-ray and canal-ray experiments and was discovered last, by Chadwick in 1932. Build the comparison table in this order — name, symbol, charge, mass, discoverer, location — and it will serve every later chapter on atomic structure. Exam takeaway: protons and neutrons sit in the nucleus and account for nearly all the mass; electrons supply the equal and opposite charge that keeps a neutral atom neutral. Self-check: state the charge and mass of each particle from memory, then explain why an atom with 17 protons and 17 electrons shows no net charge.

Read the three observations against their conclusions the way the mark scheme does: most alpha particles passed straight through the foil — so most of the atom is empty space; a few were deflected through small angles — so the positive charge is concentrated, not spread out; about one in several thousand bounced back nearly along its path — so a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus sits at the centre. Then state the two failures that demanded a better model: an orbiting electron should continuously radiate energy and spiral into the nucleus, and the model cannot explain why glowing gases emit sharp line spectra instead of a continuous rainbow. Exam takeaway: the gold foil experiment established the nucleus; it says nothing about the paths electrons follow. Self-check: reproduce all three observations with their conclusions, and name one phenomenon that Rutherford's model cannot explain.

Run three exam-standard cases until the method is automatic: aluminium oxide gives Al³⁺ and O²⁻, crossed to Al₂O₃ with no reduction needed; calcium hydroxide gives Ca²⁺ and OH⁻, crossed with brackets to Ca(OH)₂; ammonium phosphate gives NH₄⁺ and PO₄³⁻, crossed with brackets to (NH₄)₃PO₄. When both valencies share a common factor, divide first — barium oxide, from Ba²⁺ and O²⁻, must simplify to BaO, never Ba₂O₂. Exam takeaway: cross the valencies, bracket each polyatomic ion before crossing, reduce to the lowest whole-number ratio, and check the final formula is electrically neutral. Self-check: write the formulae of magnesium chloride, sodium sulphate and calcium carbonate from valencies alone, then verify neutrality by adding up the positive and negative charges.

Fill the first twenty elements as a drill: hydrogen (Z = 1) goes 1; carbon (Z = 6) goes 2, 4; chlorine (Z = 17) goes 2, 8, 7; calcium (Z = 20) goes 2, 8, 8, 2. Watch where the octet cap bites: potassium, Z = 19, is 2, 8, 8, 1 and never 2, 8, 9, because the outermost shell can hold at most 8 electrons no matter what 2n² allows. Notice also how the already-full outer shells of neon (2, 8) and argon (2, 8, 8) explain why the noble gases react with almost nothing. Exam takeaway: capacity 2n² per shell, filled in the order K → L → M → N, with a strict maximum of 8 electrons in the outermost shell. Self-check: write the configurations of oxygen, sodium and potassium, and state what each configuration predicts about the element's valency.

Add the ammonia check to lock the law in: in every sample of ammonia, nitrogen and hydrogen stand in a fixed 14 : 3 mass ratio — synthesised in a laboratory plant, extracted from a fertiliser bag, or released by bacteria in soil, the ratio never drifts. Contrast a mixture deliberately: stir 1 g of salt into 10 g of water while a friend stirs 3 g into 10 g — both are perfectly good salt solutions, because mixtures carry no fixed recipe by nature. Exam takeaway: a compound has a fixed composition by mass wherever it is found; a mixture's composition is flexible, and that single contrast separates the two categories. Self-check: state the hydrogen-to-oxygen mass ratio in water, then calculate the mass of oxygen required to burn 2 g of hydrogen completely.

Line the technique up against simple evaporation so the comparison question never catches you: evaporation to dryness destroys the crystal shape, and any soluble impurity deposits mixed into the solid, while crystallisation keeps soluble impurities dissolved in the mother liquor and grows pure, well-shaped crystals on slow cooling. Name the steps in order — dissolve in minimum hot water, filter while hot, concentrate to a saturated solution, cool slowly, decant the mother liquor, dry the crystals — and quote the standard uses: purifying copper sulphate and alum in the lab, and obtaining sugar and common salt on the industrial scale. Exam takeaway: crystallisation separates a pure solid from its impure solution by using the change of solubility with temperature; slow cooling is what makes the crystals pure and large. Self-check: explain why the solution is filtered while still hot, and why crystals grown by slow cooling differ from the crust left by evaporation to dryness.

Note the two conditions the effect depends on: the particles must be comparable in size to the wavelength of visible light (roughly 400–700 nm), and they must differ in refractive index from the surrounding medium. Both together make the beam visible — that is why fog dims headlights, why a searchlight beam can be seen from the side on a misty night, and why a projector beam shows up in a chalk-dusty classroom. Exam takeaway: a visible light path inside a dispersion is direct evidence of colloidal particles; a true solution leaves the beam invisible, and a suspension merely looks murky without a defined bright cone. Self-check: predict, with a one-line reason each, what a laser pointer does when shone through salt solution, milk and muddy water.

Weigh the theory against its own postulates, exactly as the exam expects: indivisibility fell when electrons, protons and neutrons were discovered; identical mass for all atoms of an element fell with the discovery of isotopes; and identical atoms across different elements fell with isobars. What survives untouched is the explanatory core — atoms still rearrange without being created or destroyed in chemical reactions, which is why mass is conserved, and compounds still form in fixed simple whole-number ratios, which is why composition stays constant. Exam takeaway: state the postulates, then judge each against the evidence; a theory can be wrong in its details and still lay the foundation of a science. Self-check: name the postulate that isotopes disprove, the one that isobars disprove, and one postulate that remains valid today.

Drill the five exam favourites in one sweep: sodium (2, 8, 1) has valency 1; magnesium (2, 8, 2) has valency 2; oxygen (2, 6) has valency 8 − 6 = 2; nitrogen (2, 5) has valency 8 − 5 = 3; neon (2, 8) has valency 0. The oxygen error is the classic one — six outer electrons tempt the answer 6, but oxygen completes its octet far more easily by gaining two electrons than by losing six, so its valency is 2. Exam takeaway: count the outermost-shell electrons; up to four, valency equals the count, five or more, valency is eight minus the count, and a completely full outer shell means valency zero. Self-check: write the configuration and valency of aluminium, sulphur and argon, and predict the formula each would form with hydrogen.

Arrange the three models on one timeline and let each failure point to its successor: Thomson's spread-out positive charge could not survive the alpha-particle backscattering observed in 1911, so Rutherford concentrated the charge into a nucleus; Rutherford's orbiting electrons should have radiated energy continuously and collapsed into the nucleus, and the model said nothing about the sharp coloured lines of glowing gases, so Bohr allowed only fixed energy orbits in which electrons do not radiate; Bohr's orbits then faltered beyond hydrogen — multi-electron atoms and the wave-like behaviour of the electron needed the quantum mechanical model. Exam takeaway: each model failed on a specific observation, and naming that observation is what the question rewards. Self-check: state one experimental fact that each of the three models cannot explain.

Practise the three concentration expressions on numbers that check mentally: 10 g of glucose dissolved in 90 g of water is a 10 % mass-by-mass solution, because 10/(10 + 90) × 100 = 10; 5 g of salt made up to 100 mL of solution is 5 % mass-by-volume; 20 mL of ethanol made up to 100 mL with water is 20 % volume-by-volume. Note the classic trap in mass-by-mass — the denominator is the mass of the whole solution, solute plus solvent, never the solvent alone. Exam takeaway: use whichever expression the question names, keep the denominator equal to the total solution, and write the formula before substituting numbers. Self-check: calculate the mass of solute in 250 g of a 15 % mass-by-mass solution, and state the answer in a single line.
